title: What is a JVM shutdown hook? When does Runtime.addShutdownHook run, when does it NOT run (kill -9), and how do you use it for graceful shutdown?
shortTitle: JVM shutdown hook — Runtime.addShutdownHook for graceful shutdown
topicTitle: What is a JVM shutdown hook? When does Runtime.addShutdownHook run, when does it

s1_definition.profdef: A JVM shutdown hook is a registered thread that the JVM runs when it begins an orderly shutdown. You register it with `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread)`. It runs when the last non-daemon thread finishes, when `System.exit` is called, or when the process receives an orderly termination signal such as SIGTERM or Ctrl-C (SIGINT). It does NOT run on an abrupt kill such as `kill -9` (SIGKILL) or a hard JVM crash, because the operating system destroys the process immediately. Hooks are used for graceful shutdown: flushing buffers, closing connections, draining in-flight work, and releasing resources. They must be fast and must not assume unlimited time.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India closes for the day, the manager rings a bell and staff finish the customer they are serving, lock the vault, and switch off the lights. That orderly closing is the shutdown hook. But if the building suddenly loses all power (kill -9), nobody gets to finish anything — the lights just go out. So the hook only helps for a polite closing, not a sudden blackout.
s1_definition.oneliner: A shutdown hook runs on an orderly stop (SIGTERM, System.exit, Ctrl-C) but never on kill -9, so use it for fast graceful cleanup, not guaranteed work.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A JVM shutdown hook is a registered thread that the JVM runs when it begins an orderly shutdown. You register it with `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread)`. It runs when the last non-daemon thread finishes, when `System.exit` is called, or when the process receives an orderly termination signal such as SIGTERM or Ctrl-C (SIGINT). It does NOT run on an abrupt kill such as `kill -9` (SIGKILL) or a hard JVM crash, because the operating system destroys the process immediately. Hooks are used for graceful shutdown: flushing buffers, closing connections, draining in-flight work, and releasing resources. They must be fast and must not assume unlimited time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India closes for the day, the manager rings a bell and staff finish the customer they are serving, lock the vault, and switch off the lights. That orderly closing is the shutdown hook. But if the building suddenly loses all power (kill -9), nobody gets to finish anything — the lights just go out. So the hook only helps for a polite closing, not a sudden blackout.

**One line to remember:** A shutdown hook runs on an orderly stop (SIGTERM, System.exit, Ctrl-C) but never on kill -9, so use it for fast graceful cleanup, not guaranteed work.

sections.s2_technical:
You register a hook with `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> cleanup()))`. The thread must be created but not started; the JVM starts it during shutdown. You can register multiple hooks and the JVM runs them concurrently in unspecified order, so hooks should be independent of each other.

The hook runs in three orderly cases: when all non-daemon threads complete normally, when any thread calls `System.exit(code)`, and when the OS sends a terminable signal like SIGTERM (what Kubernetes sends before killing a pod) or SIGINT from Ctrl-C. In all these, the JVM pauses to run every registered hook before finally exiting.

The hook does NOT run for SIGKILL (`kill -9`), a power loss, or a hard crash of the JVM itself such as a native segfault, because the process is torn down without the JVM getting control. This is why you must never rely on a hook for correctness-critical persistence; it is best-effort cleanup only. Important data must be committed transactionally as you go, not deferred to shutdown.

Hooks must be fast and robust. Orchestrators give a limited grace period (Kubernetes defaults to thirty seconds between SIGTERM and SIGKILL), so a slow hook gets cut off by the following SIGKILL. A hook should not start new long work, should not call `System.exit` again (which can deadlock the shutdown), and should catch its own exceptions so one failing hook does not stop the JVM from exiting. A common pattern is to flip a running flag to false, stop accepting new requests, wait a bounded time for in-flight work to finish with `executor.awaitTermination`, then close resources.

A senior-level nuance is coordinating hooks with executors. You typically call `executor.shutdown()` to stop accepting new tasks, then `awaitTermination` with a timeout, and if that times out, `shutdownNow()` to interrupt stragglers. You also set a bounded wait so the hook itself cannot exceed the orchestrator's grace window.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a payment processor as a long-lived service. When the deployment system rolls out a new version, it sends SIGTERM to the old pod. If the service just died instantly, any payment currently being written would be left half-done and the audit log buffer would be lost. This is exactly what a shutdown hook fixes — it gives the service a chance to finish in-flight payments and flush the audit buffer before exiting.

Problem 2 — Operators sometimes do an emergency `kill -9`. The team must understand that the hook will not run then, so the service must also persist each payment transactionally as it happens, not only at shutdown. This is exactly the best-effort nature of hooks.

The project is a payment processor with a graceful shutdown. `PaymentProcessor` accepts payments on a thread pool and keeps a `running` flag. A registered shutdown hook flips `running` to false, stops accepting new payments, waits a bounded time for in-flight payments to finish, flushes the audit buffer, and closes the pool. The demo submits payments, then triggers shutdown to show the hook draining work cleanly.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run — press Ctrl-C to see the hook drain gracefully (SIGINT)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.payment.ShutdownHookDemo

# Send SIGTERM to a running process (hook RUNS)
kill -TERM <pid>

# Send SIGKILL — hook does NOT run, process dies instantly
kill -9 <pid>
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three payments submitted, then the JVM begins to exit (same path as SIGTERM).

Step 1 — The processor is constructed and registers its graceful shutdown hook with the Runtime. The hook thread is created but not started.

Step 2 — Three payments are submitted to the pool. Each takes about 200 milliseconds and records an audit entry as it completes. Payments persist as they go, not at shutdown.

Step 3 — Main finishes. Because the only remaining work is the pool, the JVM begins orderly shutdown and starts the registered hook thread.

Step 4 — The hook sets `running` to false so no new payments are accepted, then calls `pool.shutdown()` to let in-flight payments finish. It waits up to ten seconds with `awaitTermination`.

Step 5 — The in-flight payments complete and record their audit entries. The hook calls `audit.flush()` to push buffered entries to durable storage, then logs completion and the JVM exits.

Final output:

```
INFO: Processed payment SAV2001→CUR3001 50000
INFO: Processed payment CUR3001→SAV2001 12000
INFO: Processed payment SAV2001→CUR3001 8000
INFO: Shutdown hook started — draining payments
INFO: Flushing 3 audit entries to durable store
INFO: Graceful shutdown complete
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Signal / exit event
    │
    ├─ SIGTERM (k8s), SIGINT (Ctrl-C), System.exit, last non-daemon done
    │        │
    │        ▼
    │   JVM starts shutdown hook thread
    │        │ running = false  (reject new payments)
    │        │ pool.shutdown()  (finish in-flight)
    │        │ awaitTermination(10s)  ── timeout? → shutdownNow()
    │        │ audit.flush()    (best-effort)
    │        ▼
    │   JVM exits cleanly
    │
    └─ SIGKILL (kill -9) / crash / power loss
             │
             ▼
        process destroyed — HOOK NEVER RUNS
        (in-flight payment half-done unless already committed)
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
A JVM shutdown hook is a thread I register with Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook, and the JVM runs it when it begins an orderly shutdown. That happens in three cases: when the last non-daemon thread finishes, when some code calls System.exit, or when the operating system sends a terminable signal like SIGTERM, which is what Kubernetes sends before it kills a pod, or SIGINT from Ctrl-C. In all of those the JVM pauses and runs every registered hook before it finally exits.

The critical thing I always say is when the hook does not run. It does not run on a hard kill, which is kill -9 or SIGKILL, and it does not run on a power loss or a native crash of the JVM, because in those cases the process is destroyed instantly and the JVM never gets control. That is why a shutdown hook is strictly best-effort cleanup and I never rely on it for correctness. Anything that must be durable, like a committed payment, I commit transactionally as it happens, not deferred to shutdown.

I use hooks for graceful shutdown. The pattern is to flip a running flag to false so the service stops accepting new work, then shut down the executor so in-flight tasks finish, wait a bounded amount of time with awaitTermination, and if that times out, call shutdownNow to interrupt the stragglers, and finally flush buffers and close connections. The hook must be fast, because an orchestrator gives a limited grace period, thirty seconds by default in Kubernetes, and then sends SIGKILL anyway, so a slow hook gets cut off. The hook should also catch its own exceptions and must not call System.exit again.

At National Bank of India our payment processor runs as a long-lived service, and during rolling deployments the platform sends SIGTERM to the old pod. Our shutdown hook stops accepting new payments, drains the in-flight ones within a bounded window, flushes the audit buffer, and closes the database pool, so a deploy never leaves a payment half-written. We also persist each payment transactionally as it is processed, precisely because an operator doing an emergency kill -9 would skip the hook entirely. The sentence I give interviewers is that a shutdown hook runs on an orderly stop like SIGTERM, System.exit, or Ctrl-C but never on kill -9, so I use it for fast, best-effort graceful draining and I rely on transactional commits, not the hook, for anything that must survive.
